display: I'm trying to understand where GenerativeAI is taking the software industry as a whole. I work mostly at the small org level 30-200 people, with 5-10 teams building software products. I would like to take a systems thinking approach
The broader market expects a speedup. I can see it is faster to generate code. I don't think the broader market understands the downstream effects of creating more code faster.
I think the first three are interlinked.

Using our Systems Thinking hat, ask questions to get the heart of the problem in this story: Marcus is a senior architect at a mid-sized software company where development is organized into horizontally specialized teams—database administrators in one group, front-end developers in another, a dedicated reporting team, and so on. He's currently embedded with a project that sits at the center of the company's ecosystem, connecting to what feels like an absurd number of external systems: payment processors, third-party APIs, legacy databases, and several internal platforms maintained by other departments.
When the project kicked off, Marcus raised concerns about the team structure. The Scrum Master, trying to bring order to the complexity, decided to split the work: one team would focus on delivering user-facing stories while a second team handled the technical integrations and interface work. It seemed logical on paper—let each group play to their strengths.
Six sprints later, Marcus describes what's unfolding as a "vicious death spiral."
Refinement and planning sessions now routinely stretch past eight hours. Stories arrive at these meetings incomplete, missing critical details about how they'll interact with the technical layer. The integration team, trying to be thorough, launches into deep technical discussions that the story team can't fully follow. Meanwhile, the story team keeps surfacing requirements that expose new integration challenges nobody anticipated. Dependencies ping-pong between the groups, and nobody feels confident enough to commit to estimates.
Marcus has watched team members check out mentally around hour five. He's seen the same story carry over across three sprints because the slicing never quite works. The Scrum Master keeps extending the sessions, believing that more time will eventually surface all the hidden complexity.
Marcus is convinced there has to be a way to groom, slice, and size stories in under ten minutes. He just can't see how to get there from here.
They're trying to create a more efficient team. The assumption is each group will specialize and work faster in their own context.
